nutshell: Automated gorilla population monitoring from camera-trap footage is bottlenecked by manual video review and a lack of large-scale in-the-wild datasets. GorillaWatch introduces three new gorilla video datasets plus an end-to-end detect-track-reID pipeline, and finds that aggregating static image-foundation-model (DINOv2) features via a transformer aggregation module beats dedicated video architectures for this data-scarce re-ID task, with multi-frame self-supervised pretraining giving further gains.
contributions: Three new datasets: Gorilla-SPAC-Wild (160,818 samples from 1,371 tracklets across 738 in-the-wild camera-trap videos, 137 individuals - the largest in-the-wild primate re-ID video dataset to date), Gorilla-Berlin-Zoo (cross-domain evaluation set, 5 individuals, 153 videos), and Gorilla-SPAC-MoT (25 videos with dense frame-by-frame MOT annotations split into Easy/Hard by interaction density).

A multi-frame self-supervised pretraining strategy that extends DINOv2's multi-crop augmentation to sample crops across time within a tracklet rather than from a single image, giving up to 11% re-ID accuracy gains over single-frame pretraining baselines.

A differentiable adaptation of AttnLRP for non-differentiable k-NN retrieval, via three proposed proxy scores (Similarity, Proto Margin, k-NN Margin) that let the authors verify via attribution maps that the fine-tuned model relies on biometric traits (face, body shape) rather than background/vegetation shortcuts.

A systematic architecture comparison showing temporal aggregation of static image-foundation-model features (their PTAM module: 73.06% top-1 on SPAC-Wild) substantially outperforms end-to-end video architectures adapted for re-ID (InternVideo2: 39.51%; TimeSformer even with a DINOv2 backbone: 38.27%).

A constrained clustering approach for unsupervised population size estimation that adds cannot-link constraints (same-frame, same-location-same-time, different social group) to standard clustering algorithms, sharply reducing over-segmentation versus unconstrained clustering.
deficiencies: The paper's own Table 1 ablation shows their specialized Gorilla re-ID appearance model reduces tracking Identity Switches only from 7.17 (no re-ID) to 6.75, and is statistically indistinguishable from plugging in off-the-shelf DINOv2-Giant (6.92) - the text frames this as evidence that occlusion makes appearance features 'ambiguous or unavailable,' but it also means their own trained re-ID model adds almost no measurable value to the tracking pipeline it's bundled into.

The constrained-clustering population counting method that works well on Gorilla-SPAC-Wild (465→17 clusters via HAC, true K=16) is dramatically less effective on Gorilla-Berlin-Zoo (2277→156 clusters, true K=5) - the paper attributes this to the zoo having only one social group, but this means the proposed method is largely unusable in exactly the kind of controlled/enclosure deployment (zoo, sanctuary) where population counting would otherwise be easiest, and depends heavily on wild-specific metadata (multiple camera sites, social group labels) that many camera-trap deployments won't have.

The headline finding that video architectures underperform (Table 2) is potentially confounded by unequal tuning effort: the DINOv2 image pipeline receives extensive, explicitly-described hyperparameter tuning (100 epochs, L2/L2SP regularization search, cosine LR schedule tuning in Sec 5.1.1), while AIM/TimeSformer/InternVideo2 are described only via architecture and initialization choices with no equivalent tuning detail - the paper's own hypothesis that video models need 'a dedicated video-aware pretraining stage' is proposed but never tested, leaving open how much of the gap is architectural versus a tuning-budget artifact.

All results are single-run with no reported variance across seeds, and several evaluation splits are very small (16 test individuals for Gorilla-SPAC-Wild, only 5 individuals total for Gorilla-Berlin-Zoo) - top-1 accuracy differences of a few points between methods (e.g., PTAM 73.06 vs. Embedding Averaging 70.08) are hard to interpret as robust without any confidence intervals.
notable: The three differentiable proxy scores for explaining k-NN retrieval decisions (Similarity, Proto Margin, k-NN Margin) are a reusable technique for auditing any embedding-based retrieval/re-ID system with attribution methods originally built for classifiers with continuous logits - useful beyond wildlife monitoring wherever a deployed re-ID system needs to demonstrate it isn't relying on background/shortcut features. Also notable as a broader negative result: simple embedding averaging (70.08% top-1) comes close to their best method (PTAM, 73.06%) while comfortably beating every purpose-built video transformer tested (22-39%), reinforcing that in data-scarce re-ID domains generally, reaching for a video-native architecture may not pay off relative to just aggregating a strong pretrained image backbone's per-frame features.
